Oct 14 : ASML on Wednesday forecast fourth-quarter sales above analyst expectations, as AI-driven demand for its chipmaking equipment remains strong, and narrowed its 2026 outlook. The Dutch company guided for fourth-quarter net sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion ($15.9 billion to $17.0 billion) and a gross margin of around 57 per cent. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected sales of €14.19 billion and a gross margin of 55.4 per cent. ($1 = 0.8924 euros)

FAST

BEIJING: China's export growth topped forecasts in September, with robust overseas demand helping offset weak consumer spending and easing pressure on policymakers to deliver this year's growth goal. Resilience in goods exports has for a second year defied pressure from Western countries seeking more balanced trade with China, keeping factories humming and shoring up economic growth against subdued domestic demand and investment. Exports in September soared 36.3 per cent from a year earlier, outstripping August's 25.0 per cent rise and far exceeding expectations for 25.5 per cent growth, customs data showed on Wednesday. September's growth was the fastest since February this year when exports expanded 39.6 per cent. Imports jumped 31.0 per cent, compared with 28.2 per cent growth in August and economists' forecasts of a 24.5 per cent gain.

China's trade surplus reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of the year, putting the manufacturing powerhouse on course to surpass US$1 trillion in surplus sooner than last year unless exports slow sharply in the final quarter. For now, such a slowdown appears unlikely. A deal with the European Union to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc, announced earlier this month, is likely to weigh on China's booming auto trade over time. But with the trade measures likely being laid out in December, exporters may drive up shipments to beat the deadline. President Xi Jinping's September summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington secured an extension to their tariff truce and an agreement to cut tariffs on US$30 billion worth of goods from each side. With the global build-out of AI infrastructure showing little sign of slowing, analysts expect demand for Chinese-made technology products, including semiconductors, to remain robust. China's factory-gate prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September, separate data showed, while consumer inflation edged up but lagged forecasts, underscoring an uneven recovery. The strength in exports, however, indicates that policymakers could still bank on moderate policy support to meet China's 4.5 per cent to 5 per cent annual GDP growth target. The Canton Fair, China's largest trade exhibition, will kick off on Thursday for Chinese manufacturers to showcase their wide array of products to foreign buyers. Going forward, risks of curbs on Chinese exports loom as China continues to defend its industrial and monetary policies, which Washington and Brussels blame for Beijing's massive trade surplus. China's central bank last week pushed back against criticism of its exchange-rate policy with a lengthy policy statement, arguing that it never pursued competitive depreciation and rejecting claims that China keeps the yuan artificially weak to gain a trade advantage. As exports now serve as a key growth engine, any major hit to the sector could in turn prompt policymakers to step up stimulus measures to address weak domestic demand and the years-long property market downturn.

Source: Reuters/ec

FAST

BANGKOK, Oct 14 : The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday issued an urgent call for advanced economies and others to reduce government spending, cut deficits and lower debt levels, warning that delays would only make the job harder in coming years. Rodrigo Valdes, head of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs department, said rising sovereign bond yields were adding to fiscal pressures at a time when average public debt was poised to hit 100 per cent of gross domestic product, the highest seen since World War Two, leaving countries with less margin for delay. "We're saying now it's urgent and it's now because basically the conditions have changed," Valdes said, noting the risks posed by inflationary pressures, high levels of global debt and rising sovereign bond yields. "So, if you want one message, we dialed up the urgency of our message."

Ahead of this week's annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Valdes had told Reuters that "the fiscal results this year are worse than expected six months ago, and worse than they were one year ago." The majority of countries were now looking at boosting spending instead of tightening their belts, he said.  NEED TO BUILD POLITICAL SUPPORT Valdes said the challenge for major advanced economies with high debt levels was to build political support for concrete plans to contain borrowing costs in the medium term, and limit spillovers to the rest of the world. "The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes," the IMF said in a blog released on Wednesday. Delaying adjustments would lead to increasing interest burdens and fiscal vulnerabilities, further narrowing policy options. Financing conditions for many emerging market and developing economies had remained favorable, but might not last, the IMF said, urging those countries to also reduce their fiscal vulnerabilities and strengthen debt management. Low-income countries, where external financing was already tighter, needed to strengthen their tax systems and improve spending efficiency, the IMF said. High oil prices, persistent inflation, stronger investment demand and higher-than-expected AI growth have driven sharp increases in long-term sovereign yields in recent months. The Group of Seven's average 10-year government bond yield rose over 110 basis points between February and September, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF said. The IMF said the effective average cost of government financing was projected to rise to 3.7 per cent by 2031 from 2.3 per cent in 2021. In the US, interest payments were expected to reach 5.3 per cent of GDP, up from 2.8 per cent of GDP before the COVID pandemic, roughly equal to its projected expenditure on Social Security.  That number was even higher in low-income countries, where interest payments today consume over 15 per cent of tax revenues, compared to an average cost of around 9 per cent between 2011 and 2019. Adding to the stress, governments in advanced economies were refinancing more debt at shorter maturities, causing higher rates to pass through to government costs more quickly, the IMF said. For the G7 and Spain, it said, the share of debt maturing within one year was now approaching 30 per cent. Inflation rates above target and higher energy prices meant central bankers would likely need to keep rates higher for longer, which in turn would limit governments' ability to respond to downturns, just as demands for increased spending on defense, energy security and aging populations were mounting. The IMF said interest rates on debt also now exceeded expected nominal growth rates in a number of countries, which would make it even harder for them to stabilize debt. Valdes said more countries were allowing higher energy prices to pass through, but many were still relying on costly, broad-based measures to shield their populations.  "Our estimate is that taken together, the fiscal cost of all these measures is about one half percent of global GDP (gross domestic product)," he said, noting that a continuation of such measures would drive prices higher at the global level.

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 14 : SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won has agreed the sale of a 1.34 per cent stake in holding company SK Inc to an investment fund linked to Dell Technologies founder Michael Dell for 544 billion won ($406 million), a regulatory filing showed on Wednesday. The deal is part of Chey's plan to raise 944 billion won through share sales to pay a divorce settlement to his former wife.  Here are some details:  • The buyer of 972,493 SK Inc shares was identified as DFO Public Investments, L.P., a Delaware-based investment fund affiliated with DFO Management, the family investment office of Michael Dell, according to the filing and DFO Management's website.

Of those, 681,431 shares, or 0.94 per cent, will be sold to Korea Investment & Securities for 400 billion won. • SK had previously identified the buyer of the remaining shares only as a strategic investor, saying the investor had agreed to buy the stake after considering SK Inc's business competitiveness and medium- to long-term growth prospects. • Dell Technologies, a major supplier of AI servers and data centre infrastructure, has business ties with SK Hynix, SK Group's memory chipmaking unit. The stake is being acquired by a Dell family investment fund, rather than Dell Technologies itself. • Reuters reported in May that global technology companies had approached SK Hynix with proposals to invest in dedicated memory chip production lines and help finance costly manufacturing equipment as they sought to secure supplies amid booming AI demand. • The Korea Corporate Governance Forum said Chey and the buyers would be required to disclose their stakes as joint holdings if they had agreed, even informally, to exercise their voting rights in the same way. Failure to do so would violate South Korea's capital markets law, it said. • The forum, an independent watchdog that monitors corporate governance issues in South Korea, said a strategic investor suggested their interests could be aligned, raising the possibility that the fund could be deemed a joint holder with Chey under the law. FAST

HONG KONG, Oct 14 : Asian shares inched higher on Wednesday as those related to artificial intelligence found respite after a selloff, while any gain was tempered by elevated oil prices and caution ahead of U.S. inflation data later in the global day. Among firms in the AI supply chain, chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rose more than 2 per cent in South Korea while Kioxia was steady in Japan, recovering some of the previous session's loss. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 0.5 per cent after U.S. stocks ended the previous session with a mild loss. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.2 per cent and South Korea's Kospi added 1.8 per cent. Sentiment remained cautious, however, with oil prices elevated as concern over energy supplies intensified following Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.

U.S. crude ticked up 0.8 per cent to $94.96 a barrel. Brent crude rose to $106.6. "After yesterday's chip-led sell-off in the region ... market participants will be gauging whether shakiness across major indices eases. The geopolitical situation globally and the impact on energy markets won't help," said analyst Kyle Rodda at Capital.com. In another sign of risk aversion, longer-dated bonds rallied as investors sought safety. The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes was steady at 5.221 per cent after touching its lowest in nearly two weeks, while that on 30-year notes held at 5.569 per cent following a three-day decline. On Wall Street overnight, U.S. bank stocks lost ground after mixed quarterly earnings results from Citigroup and peers, weighing on broader markets. U.S. stock futures, the S&P 500 e-minis, were up 0.04 per cent at 7,858.8. CPI TEST AWAITED Market participants were awaiting US consumer price index data on Wednesday, hoping to extract clues on the Federal Reserve's interest-rate outlook. On average, economists estimated headline inflation accelerated to an annual 3.6 per cent in September due to rebounding energy prices, with the core CPI rising 0.2 per cent on a monthly basis. "The risk is the core CPI surprises to the upside because of strong consumer demand and higher costs, pushing up market pricing of an October Fed hike and the USD," said currency strategist Carol Kong at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Investors priced in a 22 per cent chance of an October interest rate hike ahead of the CPI data, the CME FedWatch Tool showed. New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said the Fed may need to raise its policy rate once more this year to slow inflation, but that he sees no need for hikes in 2027. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against the currencies of some major trading partners, was down at 102.17. The euro was little changed at $1.1202. Market participants were also awaiting Chinese inflation data on Wednesday, looking for signs of reviving domestic demand amid deflationary pressure.

Source: Reuters

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 14 : Oil prices climbed on Wednesday after two vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian officials told Reuters they were deploying new tactics to target ships, as Tehran seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections. Brent crude futures rose 63 cents, or 0.6 per cent, to $106.32 a barrel by 0345 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 66 cents, or 0.7 per cent, to $94.80 a barrel. Both contracts rose more than $1 in earlier trade before paring some gains. The Iranian officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. A container ship and a tanker were hit by unknown projectiles within the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday.

"The fact that Iranian officials are openly admitting to undermining US efforts to keep oil prices under control speaks volumes about the real intentions behind the so-called 'peace talks,'" said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova. "Iran is well aware of its geographical importance and the havoc higher oil prices can inflict on the global economy, and it may not shy away from using this leverage." Elsewhere, the Iran-allied Houthis attacked an administrative building belonging to state-owned oil firm Saudi Aramco in the city of Dhahran, causing a limited fire, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said on Wednesday. The group has fired ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia over the past week in retaliation for the kingdom's support of Yemeni government forces. Riyadh's international airport has been hit four times, with a strike on Saturday killing 13 people. "Supply concern stemming from conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia is driving prices higher," said Hiroyuki Kikukawa, chief strategist at Nissan Securities Investment, a unit of Nissan Securities. "However, the expectation that increased Russian diesel exports will ease market tightness is likely to limit sharp price movement in either direction," Kikukawa said, projecting WTI to trade between $90 and $100 a barrel. Last month, Saudi Arabia raised oil production despite disruptions to shipments caused by the US-Iran war. That led to a sharp production increase from OPEC+ — the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and partners including Russia — OPEC said on Tuesday. In Russia, the government said on Tuesday it did not see any direct link between peace talks with Ukraine and its deal to export diesel to the US. The comment came after Reuters reported that US envoys had told Ukrainian officials on Friday that the deal was part of an attempt to draw Russia back to negotiations for a peace settlement.

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Oct 14 : The dollar languished on Wednesday as traders awaited fresh signals on the timing for interest rate hikes to contend with persistent inflation. The greenback weakened from an 18-month high in the previous session as oil prices eased and investors reassessed the AI-fueled rally that has supported demand for US assets. The euro clung to gains as budget concerns in France kept regional bond yields elevated and markets on edge. Attention now focuses on the release of US consumer price index data as well as speeches from Federal Reserve policymakers that could clarify the outlook for interest rates. "The risk is the core CPI surprises to the upside because of strong consumer demand and higher costs, pushing up market pricing of an October Fed hike and the USD," Carol Kong, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said in a note.

The US Labor Department is due to release its CPI for September, which is expected to have risen 0.6 per cent month-on-month after increasing 0.4 per cent in August, while annual inflation is seen accelerating to 3.6 per cent from 3.4 per cent. Additionally, the Fed is due to publish its Beige Book. Traders see a 77 per cent chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, up from 51 per cent a month ago, while pricing in about 75 basis points of tightening by late 2027, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. Investors abandoned bets on a Fed rate hike later this month after two policymakers argued for gathering more evidence before deciding whether further tightening is needed, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller said inflation expectations remained "well anchored." Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin is scheduled to participate in a fireside chat in Virginia, while Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman is set to take part in talks in Bangkok. The International Monetary Fund and World Bank's annual meetings continue in Bangkok, with several appearances expected by European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde on Wednesday. The Australian dollar  strengthened 0.06 per cent versus the greenback to $0.6984, while New Zealand's kiwi  strengthened 0.09 per cent to $0.5614.

SYDNEY, Oct 14 : Commonwealth Bank of Australia CEO Matt Comyn said on Wednesday Australia must ensure more of the economic benefits created by AI remain in the country while regulation should work to build trust in the new technology.   Comyn said CBA, Australia's largest lender, is rolling out AI technologies across its banking portfolio, especially in business banking. The bank has also launched an AI chat within its banking app to selected customers that can access personal and business banking details. Comyn said AI could be the "most significant technology shift we have seen" but warned an official framework was needed as the technology rolls out at a fast pace around the world.

"Realising the AI opportunity will require regulation to keep pace," he said at the bank's annual investor meeting in Sydney. "Effective regulation should help build trust in AI while ensuring global technology companies operate in accordance with Australian laws and standards, and that more of the economic value created by AI is captured in Australia." Australia has started to toughen its approach to AI regulation after initially giving an unconditional welcome to AI companies.  The Labor government has responded to community pushback against AI and data centre development by saying it would take a tougher approach. The government has said it is preparing a wide-ranging set of AI laws to take effect from early 2027, which would include limits to water and energy use by data centres, as well as copyright protections and cybersecurity measures. Comyn said Australia's economy remained resilient, although more frequent and volatile international shocks were likely. "It will take time for higher interest rates to bring inflation back into the target range," Comyn said. The remarks come a day after minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's September meeting showed the board remained concerned about persistent inflation pressures and considered further rate hikes could be needed if price growth proved more stubborn than expected.  The central bank last month ordered a fourth interest rate rise for the year which took the official cash rate to 4.6 per cent, the highest level in 15 years. Comyn said Australia had little control over external shocks and would need to boost productivity through measures including building more homes, delivering reliable low-cost energy at scale and adopting technologies such as AI across the economy. In his address to shareholders, CBA Chair Paul O'Malley said cost-of-living pressures and higher interest rates continued to affect households unevenly, while businesses were managing elevated input costs and supply uncertainty. Succession planning remained a focus for the lender, O'Malley said, a year after telling shareholders Comyn would remain in the CEO role for at least another three years.

Oct 13 : The partial skull of a tiger-sized predator that prowled what is now the Isle of Wight off England's southern coast about 120 million years ago is giving scientists a better understanding of an enigmatic group of meat-eating dinosaurs known for running down prey and ripping them apart with massive hand claws. Researchers said the fossil belongs to a species they have named Invictibellatrix amberina, an early member of the lineage of Cretaceous Period carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans. Invictibellatrix adds to the knowledge of skull anatomy among early megaraptorans and, being the first one known from Europe, helps show how the group spread globally. Invictibellatrix is one of the smallest megaraptorans. Based on fossils of closely related megaraptorans, the researchers estimated that Invictibellatrix was about 16 feet (5 meters) long, with the weight of a large tiger. Its body may have been covered in filament-like feathers, they said. Megaraptorans were part of the group called theropods that spans all the meat-eating dinosaurs.

"Megaraptorans are very unique among theropods because they have relatively small and slender heads but had long and strong arms with massive hand claws as well as very lightly built skeletons," said Cassius Morrison, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Leeds in England and lead author of the study published in the journal Royal Society Open Science. "These characteristics imply that megaraptorans were agile hunters capable of chasing down prey and using their large arms and claws to catch them and disembowel them using their hand claws," Morrison said. The largest-known megaraptoran, named Maip, was about 33 feet (10 meters) long, inhabiting Patagonia during the twilight of the dinosaur age, about 50 million years after Invictibellatrix lived. Littler megaraptorans like Invictibellatrix may have hunted smaller prey like mammals, smaller reptiles and baby dinosaurs. Larger megaraptorans may have targeted bigger plant-eating dinosaurs like duckbilled hadrosaurs and long-necked sauropods, though probably not the biggest ones. Megaraptorans hunted in the opposite way from massive predators like Tyrannosaurus rex. Tyrannosaurus employed its large and stoutly built head, enormous teeth and incredible bite strength to kill prey, but had puny arms of little use in hunting. Invictibellatrix was not the Isle of Wight's top predator, with larger theropods around, alongside various herbivorous dinosaurs, and may have filled a role similar to a hyena today. There is a debate among dinosaur paleontologists as to where megaraptorans fit on the theropod family tree. Despite differences in how they were built and hunted, one hypothesis is that megaraptorans were closely related to tyrannosaurs, the group that included Tyrannosaurus and others that dominated the landscapes in North America and Asia later in the Cretaceous. 'UNCONQUERED FEMALE WARRIOR' Invictibellatrix means "unconquered female warrior." Morrison noted that after humble beginnings megaraptorans developed into apex predators in South America, Australia and Antarctica, becoming "the ruling queens," while the tyrannosaurs became the "tyrant kings" in North America and Asia. Scientists are trying to unravel the evolutionary history of megaraptorans. A leading hypothesis has megaraptorans originating in Asia before migrating through Europe into Africa and then on into South America, thriving until the dinosaurs were doomed by an asteroid strike 66 million years ago. This hypothesis was lacking fossil evidence because no megaraptorans had been known from Europe until now. "These findings help to uncover the evolution of one of the most mysterious theropod groups," University College London doctoral student and study co-author Charlie Scherer said. The Invictibellatrix fossil, a fragmented braincase, was discovered about a century ago and acquired by the Natural History Museum in London in 1924. "It was left in one of the collection's drawers ever since, and no one noticed it until a couple of years ago," Scherer said. While Tyrannosaurus may be more imposing than Invictibellatrix, the researchers noted that if a person were somehow transported back in time — like in the recent film "The End of Oak Street" — Invictibellatrix might present more of a danger. "A smaller theropod like Invictibellatrix would likely have been a much bigger threat to a human than something like T. rex because we would likely be too small for T. rex to see as a worthwhile meal because of how massive it was and the amount of energy it would be required to catch us," Morrison said. "But we would be the perfect size for something smaller like Invictibellatrix, as we are about a third to a quarter of its weight, making us a good hearty meal and more than just a snack. Additionally, Invictibellatrix would have the agility and maneuverability to pursue and catch a human."

Source: Reuters

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 14 : SoftBank's promise to pay its highest-ever yields in a record $11 billion junk-bond offering highlights the pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to secure returns on his all-in bet on AI amid concerns about possible overheating in the market. The SoftBank debt issuance last month added to a sharp surge in corporate borrowing this year, including major bond sales from Amazon.com, Alphabet and Tencent. The scale of Son's investments, which include backing totalling $64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, in particular, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. Those fresh investments are now coming under sharper scrutiny by analysts and investors amid worries about the degree of concentration in SoftBank's portfolio and whether a payoff from the expenditures by AI companies will come soon enough.

SoftBank previously sold shares in Nvidia and T-Mobile US to fund its investments, but it is now borrowing at record yields of up to 9.75 per cent in order to retain assets that it believes will appreciate, a senior SoftBank executive told Reuters. "We've borrowed money in large part because we don't want to sell assets that we believe will keep rising in value," said Alex Clavel, CEO of SoftBank Investment Advisers, which manages the Vision Funds. Sam Altman's OpenAI is the core investment in the latest iteration of Son's investment strategy, following lucrative bets on Chinese tech giant Alibaba and chip designer Arm. “Given OpenAI’s appreciation to date, 9.75 per cent is still very reasonable," Clavel said. Arm's valuation has grown fivefold since it floated in 2023 and further listings from SoftBank's private AI portfolio would clarify their value and more easily allow the assets to be monetised for additional investment activity. Altman has said OpenAI will not go public this year, citing safety concerns about AI. It also faces competition from rival Anthropic and hyperscalers, as well as low-cost Chinese labs. SoftBank was previously "betting on a bunch of numbers at the roulette table. Now it's red or black, either lose everything or gain everything," MST Financial analyst David Gibson said. INCREASED SCRUTINY OF AI-RELATED FUNDRAISING  SoftBank will pay its highest-ever coupon of 9.75 per cent on a bond issued last month that matures in 2034. That return compares with Alphabet offering 5.2 per cent for a bond issued in August that matures in 2033. SoftBank's shares surged to a record high of 8,632 yen in June, though they have fallen 38 per cent since then, while its credit default swap spreads - the cost to insure its debt against a default or other credit event - jumped 24 per cent over the same period. SoftBank's higher yields reflect investor perceptions of their risk and concentration in large positions, analysts say. "The bets are much bigger than we've ever seen," said Amir Anvarzadeh of Asymmetric Advisors, who recommends shorting the stock. James Athey, a fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough, said the fund was not allocating to high-yield bonds at this stage of the credit cycle, given current tight spread levels.   "SoftBank is so aggressive, so concentrated and so all-in, I don't think we'd be looking there first anyway," he said. Clavel, however, says SoftBank's OpenAI backing reflects their deep business ties.  "We see OpenAI as a partner, building a relationship that can deliver strategic value as well as financial returns," he said. OpenAI is also an investor in and customer of data centre company SB Energy,  which SoftBank is looking to list and may seek a valuation of $50 billion, Reuters has reported. "SoftBank is taking advantage of hyper-excitement around AI-driven businesses, applying very high valuations for relatively low revenues, and they are looking to capitalize," said MST's Gibson of the potential valuation.  Son's bets have a mixed track record - his investment in Chinese tech giant Alibaba was a major success, but Son also directed $16 billion to Adam Neumann's WeWork, which ultimately went bankrupt. Other setbacks included a crash in the value of its investments as central banks moved to hike rates in 2022.   "OpenAI's value appreciation to date far exceeds the losses in our 2021 vintage investments," Clavel said. Over the decades, Son has navigated market peaks and troughs to build SoftBank into a 30 trillion yen ($189.9 billion) company. "Being priced in is a massive transformation of the workplace with AI effectively taking over a big chunk of what gets done with human brains now," said Morningstar senior equity analyst Dan Baker. "If that goes ahead it's hard to see their investments not being very successful," he said.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Oct 13 : Apple on Tuesday unveiled a smart-home hub that taps iPhone user data to make Siri more personal, but promised privacy safeguards designed to keep that information out of the company's hands. The HomeView smart-home hub, which took center stage at an event in New York, is an important test of Apple's AI strategy as it tries to close the gap with rivals Amazon and Alphabet's Google, while reinforcing its reputation for user privacy. In a series of demonstrations, Apple showed Siri AI recognizing a user's face and performing personalized tasks such as fetching recipes from text messages, finding a nearby farmer's market for missing ingredients and then updating shopping lists.  When a different member of the household steps in, the HomeView recognizes that user's face and switches to their personal data, for example fetching information from text messages about when a friend's early morning flight lands and how long it will take them to arrive, then teeing up a coffee maker a few minutes ahead of time.

The new device and Siri AI lean on the iPhone to make those personalized features happen, reflecting new CEO John Ternus' vision of Apple's best-selling product as an "intelligent personal hub" laid out at Apple's iPhone launch event last month.  Siri AI's usefulness hinges on how much it knows about a user. HomeView draws on a personal search index stored on the user's iPhone to personalize responses. "That will give you what's more relevant, what's more timely, what's important to you, because it's coming from your iPhone," Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said in an interview. PRIVACY SAFEGUARDS AND ENCRYPTION HomeView has its own operating system and runs on Apple's A18 chip, designed to process encrypted user data in a walled-off part of the chip. To access private data, a user's iPhone has to be connected to the same home network as HomeView, and no private data is stored on the HomeView device itself. Apple said none of the data is used for marketing, including first-party advertising efforts. "One of the things we talked about is not building a marketing profile," Drance said. "Our intent is to provide users a helpful experience that adheres to simplicity, being personal, being intelligent, and continuing our commitment to privacy." A key difference between Siri AI and rival systems is that it does not end each interaction with a follow-up question designed to elicit more information from the user, a practice that Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, said was a deliberate choice on Apple's part.  "For us, it's really about creating these really great products for consumers, which is why we're not in this game of getting you to engage and continue the conversation in many, many, many turns," Rincon said. HomeView also required Apple to figure out how to make Siri personal on a device shared by multiple people in communal spaces such as a kitchen. Apple demonstrated HomeView juggling requests from family members during the morning rush to school and work. While the device can recognize up to six voices and faces to show private data, Apple said it will make decisions on which user to prioritize based on who last touched the device and other factors, and that some features such as weather and thermostat controls will be available to any user. "There is a logic built in to kind of manage that experience," Drance said. "There was thought put into the nature of that communal computer sharing of the voice and the face recognition."

MEXICO CITY, Oct 13 : Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings have agreed to buy AT&T's Mexican unit for $2 billion in cash, setting up a showdown with telecoms giant America Movil and marking one of Mexico's biggest M&A deals in recent years. News of the deal, described as a "bargain" by Scotiabank, sent shares in Televisa, Mexico's largest broadcaster and the world's largest producer of Spanish-language content, surging 5 per cent in after-hours trading on the New York Stock Exchange. AT&T's Mexican unit, the country's second-largest mobile operator after America Movil's Telcel, had some 24.7 million subscribers as of December, Televisa said. The deal will give Televisa considerable scale, lifting its share of total fixed and wireless subscribers in Mexico to 19 per cent from 8 per cent, according to the Scotiabank note to clients.

"We think the low price tag and Fintech involvement is, in itself, bad news for (America Movil), as it means the new owners can focus more resources in capex," Scotiabank said. Fintech, a private investment firm and holding company owned by the Mexican billionaire David Martinez, owns 22.3 per cent of Televisa and will take a 50 per cent stake in the purchasing consortium. It is Televisa's second attempt to enter the competitive telecommunications sector, after an unsuccessful effort between 2012 and 2014. Despite Mexico's large population, its proximity to the US, and growing demand for connectivity, establishing a foothold in the sector has long proven a challenge due to high costs and fierce competition from Telcel. Scotiabank said the new venture could seek a direct-to-cell partnership with operators like Starlink to compete with Telcel, which operates twice as many connectivity towers and runs a much stronger 5G network throughout the country. For AT&T, the sale will allow it to concentrate on its US fiber and 5G businesses, as it pours more resources into "advanced connectivity" for an AI-enabled future. Shares in AT&T gained 1.6 per cent to close at $22.85. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending regulatory approvals in Mexico. The price is subject to adjustments, plus additional contractual and contingent benefits, and will be funded through available cash and non-recourse secured debt financing, Televisa said. AT&T is not the only company to depart the Mexican telecoms sector. Spanish telecoms giant Telefonica Movistar in April sold its Mexico business to a US-led consortium for $450 million as it shifts its focus onto core markets in Europe.  AT&T's Mexican unit ended 2025 with revenue of 85.4 billion pesos ($4.65 billion) and operating income of 1.4 billion pesos, Televisa said.  ($1 = 18.36 Mexican pesos)

Oct 13 : US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was. OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department.

The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins. The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said. OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi embassy in the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. "Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through September 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020. If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release. A LinkedIn profile showed that Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said. Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile. Separately, the Information reported that OpenAI was in early talks to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter. OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers after an investigation found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information. The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture in which researchers could raise safety concerns.

Source: Reuters
